The Cartographer of Small Things

There was once a mapmaker named Oduya who was very bad at his job, because he
kept mapping the wrong scale.

The King wanted coastlines. Oduya gave him a chart of every puddle on the road
to the harbour, annotated with which ones held the sky best after rain.

The King wanted borders. Oduya submitted a map of his aunt's kitchen showing
where the warm patches fell in the afternoon, and which floorboard announced
you to the household if you stepped on it wrongly.

The King wanted trade routes. Oduya provided a chart of the eleven places in
the city where you could stand and hear the sea, marked in a blue ink he had
made himself from something he refused to name.

The King, who was not a cruel man but was a busy one, dismissed him.

Oduya kept mapping anyway. He mapped the shadow of the cathedral through a
whole year, so you could tell the date by where the dark fell. He mapped the
route a particular cat took across seven rooftops. He mapped, on a single
enormous sheet, every place in the city where someone had told him they had
been happy, and it took him thirty years, and the sheet was very full.

When the city burned, they rebuilt it from Oduya's maps, because the King's
maps showed only where things had been, and Oduya's showed what they had been
for.

He was ninety-one and did not understand what the fuss was about. He said he
had simply drawn what was there. He said everyone else had been drawing the
wrong scale.
